The original “Climate Week” was started in New York in 2009 by international non-profit Climate Group as a forum to discuss climate action outside official negotiations, and has since scaled up to become an important networking event for advocacy groups, community leaders, start-ups, and policy experts – as well as for corporates, whose presence at the event has increased over the years (one expert told The New York Times that it had transformed from “Burning Man for climate geeks” to the “Davos of climate”). Because it coincides with the annual UN General Assembly, New York Climate Week has a global reach, giving world leaders and business a platform for big-ticket announcements. Similar events in other countries – including those organized by the UN – tend to be more local or regional. India’s inaugural version, led by local NGO Project Mumbai in partnership with the government of Maharashtra, certainly had ambition. The event convened participants from over 30 countries, featuring more than 400 speakers and 4,000 attendees from business, local government, NGOs, and research, and included discussions on everything from waste systems to sustainable cooling solutions. The state government signed a clutch of partnerships with international bodies including C40, UNEP, and WRI, spanning urban planning, climate finance, and nature-based resilience. US-based delegates at the conference, especially of Indian origin, were taken with the potential for projects in the region, and with the palpable energy that had been missing from New York’s event the previous September, where dismay with Trump’s budgets cuts and policy reversals had dominated conversations. But India’s first Climate Week also reflected the challenges of climate action, from finance to equity, especially when that action flows from global to national or local systems in the south. The foremost problem is financing the shift away from fossil fuel-based economies and of protecting communities most at risk from the impacts of global warming. Current climate finance commitments of at least US$300 billion per year by 2035 remain far below the US$2.4 trillion that will be annually needed by developing countries, excluding China. India alone is estimated to need nearly $467 billion in additional capital expenditure through 2030 to transform the four key sectors of steel, cement, power, and road transport, according to an assessment by the Centre for Social and Economic Progress. This funding gap has been the central tension in climate negotiations between developing countries and developed countries in recent years. Most global finance also currently goes to mitigation – the reduction of warming emissions – rather than adaptation, or the preparation and defense of communities from climate impacts such as heatwaves and floods. Developing countries, which have contributed the least to warming emissions historically, are on the frontline of such impacts. Domestic finance is the prime driver of climate action in India, but New Delhi has been moving to create a national climate finance taxonomy to facilitate more external and private investments. Unlocking global capital markets was a key focus at Mumbai Climate Week, where the Maharashtra government launched several programs to facilitate investments into the state, explicitly selling Mumbai to the array of international banks in attendance as a gateway for global finance. “If climate capital must flow at scale,” said state chief minister Devendra Fadnavis, “Mumbai is ready to become a medium for that flow.” Many of the global partnerships signed were focused on urban climate, reflecting the growing recognition that cities are on the frontline of heat and other climate impacts, and that municipal governments can make for effective local partners. A question remains – who receives this finance? Critics say funds tend to go to larger players and big projects rather than local grassroots groups who are unable to, or don’t know how to access them. Another issue is that such finance, while necessary, runs the risk of creating a parallel industry of solutions rather than transforming existing development pathways. That gap was evident in Mumbai, where the same week the state government signed climate partnerships, its forest department moved to clear thousands of mangroves for a coastal road. The project wasn’t isolated; a spurt of infrastructure and construction projects has dented green cover and increased air pollution in Indian cities over the past few years. Regulations mandate pollution control and compensatory greening for such projects, but the former isn’t well enforced and the latter is often dispersed to distant locations, which is of no use to the communities affected by the loss of trees. The irony was not lost on Mumbai residents who turned up to protest at the Climate Week venue – they got to hear politicians who have ignored community opposition and encouraged private car use trot out the jargon of climate resilience, from “walkable cities” to “inclusivity.” The forum venue exemplified the gap, located in a new “planned” business district that lacks adequate public transport and green cover. For all these contradictions, India’s inaugural climate week seemed to reflect a genuine moment of transition – a shift toward regional and local mobilisation at a time of faltering global action. Economics is a driver; solar energy is now cheaper than coal in many markets, and the ability to generate it locally rather than depend on central grids or imported fuels is an advantage. The recent West Asia crisis could sharpen that calculus. The conflict disrupted India’s cooking gas supply and raised diesel and petrol prices. The crisis coincided with one of the region’s hottest summers, the high temperatures leading to strained power grids and outages even in Mumbai, whose electricity supply has historically been among the country’s most stable. In May, more than two months after the climate forum, and following an austerity call by the Prime Minister, the Maharashtra government directed officials to carpool their commutes. And in June, the business district started Public Transport Fridays to encourage employees to leave their cars behind. Whether authorities can make that work may be the first real sign of change. Vaishnavi Chandrashekhar is an award-winning science and environment journalist. She was a CASI Fall 2025 Visiting Fellow. This article was first published on India in Transition , a publication of the Center for the Advanced Study of India, University of Pennsylvania.

article_title: ‘Gangrene’: Shocking stories about Dalit life from the margins of the Punjabi imagination
sub_title: In this anthology, ‘gangrene’ is not merely the decay of body tissue but also a metaphor for the slow corrosion of a social world shaped by caste.
article_content: It was a hot May afternoon when I received the book. I tore through the parcel. A crisp shade of electric blue emerged from the dusty yellow envelope. The cover read: Gangrene . Until then, I knew gangrene only as the death and decay of body tissue. The byline read: Punjabi Dalit Short Stories , translated by Akshaya Kumar and Navdeep Singh. Gangrene. Caste. Gangrene. Caste. I had not even opened the book, yet the metaphor had already begun its work. The two words kept returning to me, refusing to leave each other. I left the book where it was and walked away. Over the next few days, it seemed to stare at me from across the room. I ran away from it. What was I running from? I wasn’t sure. Or perhaps I knew only too well. It was only weeks later that I found the courage to return to the book. By then, the stories haunted and fascinated me in equal measure. As I moved from one story to the next, the meaning of gangrene began to change. Bringing together 12 stories by various writers, translated from multiple Punjabi dialects and registers and spanning nearly five decades, the anthology compelled me to look more closely at Punjab. Much of whose dominant cultural imagination centres on agrarian abundance, celebration, valour and the historical trauma of Partition. Yet they tell only part of the story, leaving largely unexamined the caste order that has sustained them. Home to the highest proportion of Dalits of any Indian state, Punjab has always contained histories that remain at the margins of this imagination. Gangrene shifts our gaze towards those social worlds, where caste continues to organise access to land, labour, intimacy, desire, memory and violence. Read together, these stories reveal the social foundations of Punjab’s dominant cultural imagination, showing how control over land shapes labour, mobility, faith, leadership, intimacy and the making of the self. Integral to the anthology’s achievement are the translations. In their introduction, Akshaya Kumar and Navdeep Singh describe their approach as one of “affective translation”, seeking not merely verbal equivalence but the emotional, cultural and social worlds these stories inhabit. That approach feels especially resonant in an anthology where lived experience informs both the stories and their translation. By retaining terms such as seerie , lambardar and zaildar , the translators preserve the caste relations embedded within the language itself. It is perhaps fitting that the collection opens with Attarjit’s “Bathloo Chamiar”. Although his name is Sunder, the village knows him as “Bathloo Chamiar”, reducing him to his caste identity rather than his personhood. A Dalit manual labourer, he agrees to fill a roadside sinkhole for a meagre sum. Yet what lingers is not the exploitative labour itself but the way caste reshapes his understanding of dignity and recognition. Even when another labourer points out that the panchayat has tricked him into accepting far less than the work is worth, Bathloo refuses to see himself as wronged. “Our duty is to serve,” he insists. “Whatever the panchayat pays is enough.” The violence lies not only in the unequal exchange of labour for wages, but also in the way caste transforms exploitation into service and submission into virtue. When Bathloo collapses after days of dangerous labour, the villagers wonder whether he has been possessed by a spirit. It is easier to invoke the supernatural than to acknowledge caste violence. In that refusal, Attarjit reveals one of the many meanings of gangrene: not merely the decay of the body, but the slow erosion of a society’s capacity to recognise its moral failures. Attarjit’s second story, “Gangrene”, expands the anthology’s central metaphor beyond labour. Jagtar, a Dalit man, and Param, an oppressor caste Sikh woman, fall in love, believing that education, love and the egalitarian ideals of Sikhism might be enough to transcend caste. They are not. What makes the story devastating is not simply the failure of love but the gradual dismantling of belief itself. The very institutions and ideals Jagtar turns to for dignity become the sites through which caste is reaffirmed. Sikhism’s egalitarian ideals yield to caste endogamy, while education fails to deliver the life he imagined. By the end, it is not only Jagtar’s relationship that has collapsed but also his faith that dignity is possible within the existing social order. If “Bathloo Chamiar” locates gangrene in the extraction of labour, Gangrene reveals how the disease has spread to the very institutions that promise equality. If Attarjit’s stories locate gangrene in labour and institutions, Mohan Lal Phillauria’s “Cobbler’s Son” turns to the unfinished promises of social mobility. A story of memory as much as transition, it traces movement from village to city, father to son, hereditary labour to salaried employment, and caste-assigned identity to professional recognition. Yet caste accompanies the narrator into every new social world he inhabits. Having left the village for a government job, the narrator believes he has left behind “the cobbler’s son”, only to discover that the figure clings to him “like a leech” and follows him “like my own shadow.” Employment promises the dignity long denied to hereditary labour, but it cannot erase the memories and inheritances that shaped him. Phillauria does not romanticise the village or the city. The father cultivates dignity through Guru Ravidas and a refusal to disavow who he is, while the son seeks recognition through education and employment. Yet the story refuses to cast them as representatives of separate worlds. Their memories and inheritances fold into one another, revealing two generations negotiating the same caste history across changing geographies, where caste acquires new forms without losing its hold. Mobility comes at the cost of community without securing acceptance. The story asks what remains of home, kinship and belonging when caste compels one to leave in search of dignity but prevents from letting one arrive. Makhan Maan’s “Iron-Boned” turns to the complicated relationship between dignity, leadership and recognition. Structured through interconnected vignettes, the story continually revises our understanding of Magghar, casting him as neither a hero nor a villain. Though he occupies no formal position of power, village leaders repeatedly seek him out when they need access to the Dalit community, making him visible only insofar as he is useful. Maan reveals the costs of that visibility. While Magghar repeatedly risks himself for his community, Nanjo, his wife, bears its burden through debt, invisible emotional labour, backbreaking physical labour and quiet endurance. Yet even as he confronts oppressor caste power outside the home, the home remains one in which the desires and choices of the women in his family are governed through the language of family honour, violence and control. Rather than offering easy moral judgments, “Iron-Boned” becomes a nuanced meditation on the costs of dignity, leadership and visibility in a society that recognises Dalits only through utility, while exposing how the burdens of resistance are unevenly distributed within the Dalit household. Nachhatar’s “Cancer” asks what becomes of caste after education and professional success. Gurtej, a Dalit student whose brilliance is recognised by a committed teacher, becomes a renowned surgeon. Years later, he operates on his former schoolmate Simran, only for her grandfather to discover that the doctor who saved her life is the Dalit boy he had once forbidden her from befriending. Professional excellence may transform one’s occupation, but not the social imagination through which one continues to be seen. In doing so, “Cancer” unsettles the ideology of meritocracy at two levels. First, Gurtej’s extraordinary professional success fails to free him from caste, exposing the limits of excellence as a route to dignity. Second, the story questions how merit itself is produced. Gurtej’s journey begins because a teacher recognises his potential. Rather than mistaking his exceptional mobility for evidence of equality, “Cancer” asks what happens to the countless equally capable children whose brilliance is never recognised in the first place. Bhura Singh Kaler’s “Cry of the Sky” explores the intimate social worlds produced by caste, where labour, desire and power become inseparable. Lakha, a young seerie , cannot imagine himself worthy of Kaati, while Kaati is drawn to Jinder, the landlord’s son, whose caste position represents a form of power unavailable within her own world. Their desires are never free but shaped by unequal social relations. The story’s devastating conclusion reveals that what Kaati mistakes for the possibility of love is, in fact, another expression of caste power, as her aspiration is met with sexual violence. At the same time, I found myself uneasy with the narration’s sustained attention to Kaati’s body. Long before the assault, the descriptive gaze repeatedly returns to her physicality in ways that sit uneasily alongside the story’s otherwise powerful critique of sexual violence within the caste order. If “Cry of the Sky” reveals how caste extends into the intimate sphere, Prem Gorkhi’s “My Story, Everybody’s Story” reveals its violent consequences. The narrator’s final act of revenge cannot be understood apart from the caste order that destroys his family through the exploitative labour relations of the seerie system, the rape and murder of his sister, and the repeated sexual exploitation of his mother. Gorkhi portrays a social order in which the humanity of Dalit households is systematically denied. They are recognised only as a source of labour, sexual access or criminality, never as lives worthy of dignity, grief or justice. The story’s most unsettling insight lies in its ending, where the law remembers only the deaths of the dominant-caste men while the violence that produced them disappears from view. Rather than asking readers to judge the narrator's revenge in isolation, Gorkhi compels us to confront the conditions that made such violence imaginable in the first place. By the end, the story asks not simply how violence erupts, but whose suffering counts, whose testimony is believed, whose grief is recorded, and whose lives are rendered grievable within the caste order. Read together, these stories embody what Sharan Kumar Limbale describes as the aesthetics of Dalit literature, where lived experience becomes the basis of literary expression rather than something literature merely represents. Few seek neat plots or moral resolutions. Instead, they accumulate meaning through fragments, recurring images and remembered conversations, assembling a collective portrait of caste’s ordinary worlds. Running through that portrait are two competing ways of seeing Dalit life. The gaze of the oppressor castes recognises Dalits only through the roles assigned to them: labourers, political intermediaries, exceptional achievers, sexualised bodies or criminals. Against this gaze, the stories insist on full personhood. They restore history, memory, desire, interiority, contradiction and moral complexity to lives long reduced to social function. By the end of the anthology, the meaning of gangrene has shifted. It is no longer merely the decay of body tissue but also a metaphor for the slow corrosion of the social world. The disease spreads quietly, numbing moral perception until exploitation appears as duty, humiliation as tradition, exclusion as common sense and violence as an ordinary fact of life. Caste survives through this repetition until entire societies cease to recognise its violence as violence. When I first held Gangrene in my hands, I knew gangrene only as the slow death of body tissue. I understand now why I found it so difficult to open the book. By the final page, the title had come to signify something far more unsettling: the gradual erosion of a society's capacity to recognise another person's humanity. The two words that had refused to leave each other before I had read a single page, gangrene and caste, had by the end become impossible to separate. Kamna Singh is a writer, translator, visual artist and PhD researcher at the University of Delhi. Her work spans literary criticism, translation and visual storytelling, with a particular interest in Dalit literature, memory and life writing. Gangrene: Punjabi Dalit Short Stories, translated by Akshaya Kumar and Navdeep Singh, Penguin Random House India.

article_title: BJP’s unpopularity might be growing – but destruction of Opposition gives it breathing space
sub_title: The India Fix: A newsletter on Indian politics from Scroll.
article_content: Welcome to The India Fix by Shoaib Daniyal. A newsletter on Indian politics. As always, if you’ve been sent this newsletter and like it, to get it in your inbox every week, sign up here (click on “ follow ”). “I was never involved in corruption,” read the alleged suicide note of the former deputy speaker of the West Bengal Assembly, Asish Banerjee. “It was a blunder to join politics.” On Sunday morning, the body of the 75-year-old Trinamool Congress member was found hanging in a party office. Amidst widespread attacks on Trinamool party leaders after the Bharatiya Janata Party took power in May, Banerjee had also been abused in public by a worker of the Hindutva party. Just after his death, distraught members of Banerjee’s family appeared on television, stating that the entire family had left politics to ward off further attacks. Two days later, Satyendra Jain, a senior Aam Aadmi Party leader was arrested by the Delhi Police. Jain is in charge of Punjab, a state that goes to elections in a few months. This is not the first time he’s been sent to jail by the BJP. In 2022, Jain was arrested just a few months before the elections in Himachal Pradesh, a state he was overseeing for his party. Jain eventually stayed in prison for 18 months without trial. Politicians are rarely objects of sympathy. However, as these two examples show, increasingly, being an Opposition politician in India is a dangerous job. To some extent this has always been true for grassroots workers. However, this might now extend even to major leaders. Nowhere is this more stark right now than Bengal. The state has seen widespread attacks against Trinamool leaders ever since the party lost power in May. One outcome of this has been that the party now stands decimated. Almost all of its MLAs and MPs have left and aligned themselves with the BJP, some induced by carrots and some scared of the stick of being sent to prison. This has led to a bizarre outcome where almost the entire Bengal Assembly is now controlled by one party: the BJP. Bengal has always been a dangerous place to be an Opposition politician. From the ruling Congress attacking the Opposition Communists, to the Communists in power then attacking the Congress and Trinamool Congress, to the Trinamool then attacking Communist and BJP cadre, never has the state been without Opposition. Yet, the BJP seems to have managed it within a few weeks of coming to power. So bad are things now that the rump Trinamool still left behind cannot access any funds since its party bank accounts have now been frozen by the Modi government. Sad. Shocking. Dr Ashish Banerjee, 5 time AITC MLA, Ex Minister & Deputy Speaker has committed suicide. “I had nothing to do with corruption and yet all these completely false allegations to malign me…” pic.twitter.com/gwBGpFMHOQ While the BJP in Bengal has depended on a mixture of mob violence and state action to incapacitate the Trinamool, just the latter was enough for the Aam Aadmi Party in Delhi. The Modi government squeezed Delhi by taking over critical powers such as the ability to control bureaucrats . It jailed senior ministers including, for the first time in Indian history, the chief minister himself. While corruption was not the most important issue in the 2025 Delhi elections, it was for the BJP’s voters, according to data put out by the CSDS. Given that AAP leaders were jailed under allegations of corruption, this is hardly a coincidence. And while there is no immunity under India law for ministers accused of crimes, corruption allegations almost never see BJP ministers arrested . Part of this is to do with the fact that much of this action is led by Central agencies. But remarkably, even state police forces in Opposition-ruled states are unable to lock up major BJP leaders the way BJP-ruled states (such as West Bengal since May) are able to do – such is the power imbalance in Indian politics currently. Physical attacks and incarceration are the most dramatic risks that Opposition leaders face in India. But they are not the only ones. Defections in India are endemic, with the BJP using its vast financial and state powers to employ a carrot-and-stick regime to break Opposition parties. Almost every state party that the BJP has been up against – the Trinamool, Shiv Sena, AAP – finds itself splintered and its legislators crossing the aisle. Worse, Opposition parties find themselves hopelessly outspent during elections. Official data shows that the BJP’s income is nearly seven times that of the second-richest party, the Congress. And anyone with even a passing familiarity with Indian politics would know that the official data is only a part of the full picture. There has been much attention of late on so-called vote chori or vote theft, referring to widespread allegations of election rigging and voter roll fraud being conducted by the BJP using the unchecked Central government’s powers to appoint the Election Commission. However, if the Opposition is weak enough, elections are moot even if they are perfectly free and fair. If leaders are jailed or parties broken, then their ability to compete on a level-playing field with the BJP is severely reduced. An election is a zero-sum game. It is not enough for the BJP to lose support but someone else needs to gain it. We saw this in 2024, where the BJP was unpopular enough to lose its majority but the Opposition was unable to muster up the numbers to take a crack at unseating the saffron party. Eventually Modi formed a powerful ministry in spite of having to depend on a coalition. Protests and social media anger against the BJP since then show that the party’s popularity has only fallen. But the continued attacks on the Opposition give the BJP far more breathing room than it would have if the match were fairer.

article_title: ‘The truth of science is transitory, literature searches for the eternal in us’: Udayan Vajpeyi
sub_title: A Hindi writer who is also a translator, Vajpeyi says it is ‘like playing chess from both sides’.
article_content: Poet, essayist, fiction writer, translator, editor – Udayan Vajpeyi occupies a singular place in contemporary Indian literary life. Widely regarded as one of the most original voices in Hindi, his writing has consistently expanded the language’s imaginative and intellectual horizons. Some of Vajpeyi’s best-known works are Kuchh Vakya , Pagal Ganitagya Ki Kavitayen , Sudeshna , Door Desh Ki Gandh , Saatavan Button , Charkhe Par Barhat , and Patjhar Ke Paon Ki Mehndi , among others. His novel Qayas , recently translated by Poonam Saxena into English as Love Is Participation in Eternity, has introduced him to a wider readership. As a translator, he has brought writers such as Borges, Chekhov, Octavio Paz and Shuntaro Tanikawa into Hindi, opening new aesthetic and philosophical pathways for readers. Alongside his literary work, Vajpeyi spent more than four decades teaching Physiology at Gandhi Medical College, Bhopal. The coexistence of medicine and literature, science and imagination, appears to have shaped a distinctive sensibility in his writing, one deeply attentive to memory, grief, the human body and the unseen dimensions of experience. In a conversation with Scroll , Vajpeyi reflected on childhood, books, poetry, translation, literary traditions and the making of a life in literature. Excerpts from the interview: When you look back at your childhood now, what returns first: people, places, books, or silences? People wrapped in silences return first and also the vibrating absences which endlessly suck into themselves whatever enunciations were there. But let me add that silences which wrapped people of my childhood were all different from one another. For example , my mother comes to mind surrounded by an almost untouchable sacred silence which is completely different from that which surrounded my father. My grandmother was a ruthless teller of ghost stories and she lives in me quietly with her ghosts around her. What do you consider the true beginning of your life as a writer? In my childhood, it was extremely difficult for me to understand anything without either writing or pronouncing it in solitude. Words were like my sixth sense organ. I touched the world much more with them than with my fingers or lips. I, therefore, used to write diaries. They were not written to save a memory or an event for the future but to somehow be in the “present”. Was there a decisive moment, person, or book that altered your understanding of literature forever? When I was around 18 years old and was in medical college, I was deeply in love. On one such day, I heard a poem in my ears. The voice was as if coming from inside and outside too. I immediately wrote it down. With that poem, I suddenly felt, I don’t know how, that I was born to write. That was the moment which decided the kind of life I was going to live: that of a writer. You have written poetry, fiction, essays and criticism. Do you see them as separate forms, or as different expressions of one continuous search? Imagination brings its own form. Different kinds of imagination evoke different literary forms but they are, as you have suggested, continuous in their longing for truth. Yes, all forms in which I write have different shades of this emotion in common: longing. They are connected to each other through this emotion. Perhaps. Your work repeatedly returns to memory. Why does memory remain such a powerful literary and philosophical force for you? I rediscover memory in my imagination. What you are calling memory is actually the imagination, which is impregnated by my memory. Or you can say imagination in the garb of memory. It is so because I lost too many of my intimate people early in life. I go on re-creating them; rather go on giving bodies of my words to them so that they can reappear as vibrant presences. Was it Marcel Proust who said, “A writer smuggles across the border between life and death”? Writing for me is a way to bring the dead back to our surroundings in new bodies, in the bodies of words. Readers often feel your writing asks them to slow down and inhabit experiences that modern life urges us to move past. Has literature become one of the few places where reflection and silence still survive? Literature slows one down, makes one sit down and take a deep breath. It changes, as the American poet Denise Levertov said, the chemistry of the soul. This change makes the reader see her memories, desires and relationships in a new light, which gives her a deep pleasure because it brings her close to herself. You spent more than four decades teaching Physiology at Gandhi Medical College. How did medicine and the classroom shape your understanding of suffering and human vulnerability? I once happened to meet the great Mexican poet Octavio Paz. One of my gurus, a wonderful painter and thinker, Jagdish Swaminathan, was his close friend. When Paz was told by Swaminathan that I write poetry and also am a doctor, he said, “Well, both have a lot to do with suffering!” I would add that my work at Gandhi Medical College kept the sense of human vulnerability alive in me; it gave me a deep sense of mortality which my poetry, perhaps, kept alive. Coincidently its the realisation of one’s limits that gives rise to one’s ethical perspective. Awareness of one’s mortality is one such realisation. Science studies the body through certainty while literature often survives through ambiguity. Did these two worlds ever come into conflict within you? Let me tell you that the subject I was teaching, i.e. physiology, speculates about bodily processes; it too presents the body as the collection of mysteries rather than certainties. Only the poor teachers of science speak of certainties, because they have not gone into the depths of it, which contain numerous mysteries, uncertainties, etc. But let me add that the truth of science is always transitory, whereas literature searches the eternal in us. It is because of this that the theories of science become redundant in time but Kalidas’s writings remain contemporary to us even after two thousand years. Looking back, did teaching young students teach the writer something books alone could not? Teaching has an immediate effect, whereas books take time to be absorbed. Teaching gives immediate gratification to good teachers, whereas books take a long time to give any pleasure to the writer from her readers. But one thing is the same in both: the process is pleasurable and reflective. Teaching is essentially communication, whereas literature is evocation. Translation has been one of the defining dimensions of your literary life. What happens to a writer while translating another writer? Translations change the way you look at your language. It brings into the open the uniqueness of your language. And also, you learn to get rid of yourself more easily because you have to divide yourself incessantly into two writers while you translate. It’s like playing chess from both sides. You have translated Borges, Chekhov, Octavio Paz and others. Which writers from world literature transformed your imagination most deeply? I translated many world writers because I felt I should visit my language, Hindi, from different angles that translation provides. But you are asking something else. Jorge Luis Borges’s work, along with my readings of Yogvashishth, transformed the way I look at life and the world. I translated Borges and he allows no internal censors to interfere with his writing. His way of writing is the realisation of freedom. Is there a writer whom you believe the world has still not read adequately? There is a poet from Indonesia called Sapardi Djoko Damono. I heard that he has died recently. He was a great poet and his writings belong broadly to Indic civilisation , as is found in his country. But the lucidity of his imagination is remarkable. You have read extensively across South Asian and world literatures. Are there shared anxieties or recurring questions that unite writers across cultures? I have read a very good number of poets, writers, and thinkers from across the world. Unfortunately, I have read not many authors from South Asia but I have seen some wonderful cinema from here. Apichatpong Weerasethakul is my favourite filmmaker. The way he sees continuity between life and death, rather than living beings and the dead, and also man and nature is remarkable. Cinema of Won Ker-Wei too is magnificent in its portrayal of subtleties of love and togetherness. I noticed one anxiety across the cultures of the world: how to go beyond what you are. And also, how to bring the “unsayable” emotions into the realm of experience. I also noticed that writings of writers and poets across the world don’t consider the borders of their nations as the borders of their experience. In other words, they travel across borders, languages, and cultures, almost invisibly. Which writers and poets from the subcontinent remain essential to your life as a reader? Valmiki, Ved Vyas, Kalidas, Bhaas, Haal, the poet of Gathashaptshat . Let me tell you a story. I was 18 years old. Even at that tender age, I was close to my other guru, the great filmmaker Mani Kaul. I went to see him. It was in Bhopal. Mani was instrumental in the making of Dhrupad Kendra and in bringing Ustad Zia Fariduddin Dagar and his elder brother, the great Veena player Zia Mohiuddin Dagar, to Bhopal. One day, late in the evening, Mani told me a story from Yogavashishth . It was about the idiosyncratic nature of time and the truth of many kinds of realities. After listening to that story, I fell down, and a completely new insight into the idea of time and temporalities was evoked in me. Other than this, the writers who influenced me deeply are Nirmal Verma, Shrikant Verma, Marcel Proust, Renu, Roberto Juarrhoz, Krishna Baldev Vaid, Mirza Ghalib, and more recently writers like Khalid Jawed, Shamsurrehman Faruqi, Madan Soni, and Wagish Shukla. What about those writing in English? Arundhathi Roy. I feel she is not only a very lucid writer but also a very courageous one. What have you been reading recently? Are there books that have stayed with you in unexpected ways? I am reading a mid-20th-century novel called Samudra Sangam , written by the Sanskrit scholar Bholaram Bhatt. It is a fictional biography of the great poet Jagannath. It speaks of the time when there was serious competition between Dara Shikoh and Aurangzeb for the throne of India. Alongside it, I am also reading one of the last novels by José Saramago, Cain . It is a comic take on the biblical story of Cain and Abel. The short stories of Borges and Chekhov, and the poems of Nirala and Shrikant Verma, always remain with me. You belong to a remarkable literary family. Your brother Ashok Vajpeyi has been an important poet and cultural figure. How did your relationship as brothers and fellow literary practitioners shape your own journey? Ashok and I are very close. Our relationship is based less on language and literature, and more on understanding each other without saying anything. Both of us read a lot. We often talk to each other about books, ideas. Now that I am part of the Raza Foundation, we also speak to each other about ways to do certain literary or artistic events. And of course we also speak to each other about children of the family, our brothers, sisters, nephews, nieces, etc. He always stood for me in my varied literary endeavours. Allowed me to do what I wanted to. Otherwise, how many elder brothers would support their younger doctor brother to not practice medicine but take literature as a profession? His presence and support always gave me an enormous amount of creative energy to work with. My twin sons, Aasteek and Hutashan, are also poets-writers. Aasteek writes in Hindi and Hutashan in English. It might seem strange, but let me say that both these fellows are brilliant poets-writers. Does literary companionship also cause disagreements? Yes, they do. For example, there are some authors and poets whom Ashok loves but they seem intolerable to me. But no disagreement can distance us. Your engagement with visual arts has been as serious and sustained as your engagement with literature. Both painting and poetry seek the truth of oneself and attempt to evoke the same in the readers and viewers. I don’t think that art or poetry communicate much; they instead evoke the wisdom in their sahridayas (readers and viewers). This wisdom, in turn, evokes an inherent sense of ethics. But their sources may or may not be the same. Language is often treated merely as a medium of expression. For you, has language itself been a place of discovery and experience? I don’t think that language is only a medium of expression. Language in literature evokes rather than communicates the sense or senses; it also evokes memory and values. It does not give you any information but illuminates those parts of yourself which are covered in darkness. This way you find yourself in new colours. Take, for example, a haiku. It’s a very powerful form of poetry in Japan. It hardly gives any information (Ancient Pond/Frog Jumps/Splash), but it succeeds in evoking a series of insights in its readers. Much of literary criticism in India has historically borrowed from European frameworks. Do you think Indian literature has developed its own independent critical vocabulary? There are very few literary critics who are trying to develop their own ways of writing literary criticism. Wagish Shukla and Madan Soni are two such Hindi critics. One reason for this, perhaps, is the colonisation of literary criticism by different kinds of ideologies; leftists or rightists, of course, rightist ideology is weak because rightists take literature to be a fruitless thing. Like Plato, they don't throw it out of their republic, they, instead, demean it. Whereas Marxist ideology tries mostly to appropriate literature. Classical Indian aesthetics gave us concepts such as Rasa, Dhvani and Auchitya. Do these concepts remain living tools for understanding contemporary literature? I do think that concepts like Rasa, Dhvani and Auchitya remain essential insights for writers and readers. They are equally significant tools to critique a work of art, including literature. All three are organising principles of a literary text. Hindi literature has moved through several major literary movements. Looking back, do movements enrich literature or sometimes limit the freedom of individual writers? The very idea of literary movement is essentially Western. West has always imagined the movement of literature through thesis and antithesis. Indian critics tried quite clumsily to fit the literary history of Indian literatures into Western categories of literary movements. It has harmed our literary endeavour. How can an act of appropriation benefit anyone? Contemporary literary discourse increasingly privileges questions of identity and politics. How do you see the relationship between aesthetics and artistic freedom? Identity politics is the worst kind of politics human beings ever developed. In an attempt to give form to one’s identity, you have to create an opposition because identity can only be oppositional. This way, our continuity with others gets obstructed; we lose sight of multiple continuities we live with, and we end up concentrating only on giving an oppositional name to ourselves. We inadvertently cut off our numerous sources. Aesthetics is a way to go beyond identities. You don’t experience the pleasure of reading a book, what is called “anand”, if you do not get rid of your individualistic identity and feel everyone in yourself and yourself in everyone. Literature attempts to find that in human beings, which is unique and yet universal. It is through such artistic practices that one realises one’s artistic freedom. Arts and literature are like trees whose roots may be in one place but whose flowers grow for everyone in the world to smell. Did travel change your understanding of literature, or did it ultimately deepen your understanding of home and belonging? I love travelling. It takes me to places which give me completely new vantage points to look at my civilisation and cultures and languages. It is like looking at your loved one from a certain angle, from where they look completely different. Thus, the traveller cannot essentialise their homes, their cities, their countries. It’s like this: If you put green colour next to yellow, you would get a kind of yellow and if you put red colour beside the same yellow. It would look like a different yellow. In a sense, countries, cities and of course “yellows” are not the same. Has the digital age transformed the experience of reading? It has transformed it. It has made it fast and shallow. There is some kind of inherent association of reading and the touch of the paper. I sometimes feel that reading some text on digital media is like talking to a person running, whereas reading a book is like sitting with someone and talking at ease. Your essays suggest that reading is not merely an intellectual activity but a way of inhabiting the world. What makes someone a serious reader? Curiosity. Curiosity is a fundamental quality of any good reader. She has this awareness that curiosity leads to pleasure and experience of oneself. She also remains aware that curiosity would, in the end, enrich a person. The second quality of the reader is to be attentive to a text. It’s the quality of attention, my guru Mani used to say, which evokes insights in readers. You have witnessed Hindi literature across several generations. What do younger writers possess today that your generation perhaps did not, and what do you think has been lost? The younger generation is in a hurry. Most of them don’t enjoy the act of writing; instead, they enjoy only its acceptance or appreciation by their readers. Yet they are more competent in dealing with the multiplicity of languages which surround them. Some of them write extremely fast. I do think this too is important. Is there a book you wish you had written? I wish I had written Orhan Pamuk’s My Name Is Red . The way he has intertwined the narrative of the novel with the discussion on miniature paintings is most wonderful. Across your years of reading and travelling, have you encountered a writer, artist or thinker whose presence changed you more as a person than as a literary figure? There were many such persons. First was my guru Mani Kaul. He changed the way I looked at suffering and partings. Second was Nirmal Verma. He taught me to experiment with writing and made me feel the pulsations of language. Third was Jagdish Swaminathan. He changed the way I looked at paintings and Indian civilisation. In the light of his insights, I learnt to examine the colonisation of our ways of living in India. I met Navjyoti Singh, a remarkable philosopher; he too enriched me immensely with his insights into the ontology of arts and literature. Looking back on your life as a writer, translator, teacher and reader, what remains unfinished? Everything is unfinished. I wish to teach more, read a lot more, and write more. I have a few novels in my head. I also wish to translate more, particularly “abhang” of Tukaram into Hindi. If your readers 50 years from now remember only one thing about your work, what would you want that to be? I would want them to remember that there was a poet who treated time as a flexible, reconfigurable entity and tried to evoke subtle emotions through his creativity. Whose language pulsated like a throbbing wound or heart. As one grows older, certain questions become deeper and certain silences become larger. What questions stay with you today? I more and more experience the endlessness of life, of being. From childhood to now, I think about the transformations my being has gone through. I also think about why my body is growing older whereas my mind feels as if I am still no more than 18 years old, eager as ever to know whatever crosses my field of vision, so to speak.

article_title: Thinking is a sport, not a chore: Why children’s literature creators will win the war against AI
sub_title: A children’s author makes a case for rejecting AI.
article_content: Disclaimer: The following text is entirely human-authored. No “outside” help was sought to outline the piece. Editing was not outsourced to a “foreign hand”. Research was strictly restricted to gossip, Google and good ol’ social media skulking. Synonyms were deployed the old-fashioned way (many thanks, Roget’s International Thesaurus). Sentences were completed unassisted. Deadline was missed by a mile. Slap on that “100% unaided by AI” sticker already. With that out of the way, let’s get started on the much-dreaded, oft-debated, forever-relevant subject of AI. My first brush with it? Many, many decades ago. In the presence of a responsible adult. For a short story. “ AI EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE!!!!!” went a particularly excitable character from the aforementioned work of fiction. I fondly remember my English teacher’s remarks lovingly scribbled in the margins: “Way too many exclamation marks”, “Couldn’t figure out the rest. Would’ve been easier to read hieroglyphics”, and “Save doodles for art class”. Moral of the story? Using AI in creative writing does not lead to gold star glory. Cut to the present. For the longest time, I thought Gemini was a star sign. And when people claimed they were “into Gemini big time”, naturally, I assumed they were gushing about their affinity for folk born in the third sign of the zodiac. As for Claude, who can forget Phoebe Buffet-Joey Tribbiani’s iconic “Je m’appelle Claude”? Titan? Made in India brand. Llama? South American camel cousin. Rufus? Helloooo, ever watched Gossip Girl ? ChatGPT? Street food GujiyaPapdiTokri. Imagine, then, after many, many decades of this blissful, utopic, luddite-y existence, suddenly being bombarded with stuff like: “Do you think bots will replace you?” – Frantic journalists “Really think I’d use ChatGPT to write your book reviews on Amazon?” — Fawning friends and family “Why don’t you write a 10,000-word piece on AI for … <insert name of newspaper/magazine/digital platform>. ASAP. No excuses. It’ll help spread the word about your new book. Heaven knows your feeble attempts on Instagram aren’t helping.” – Fed-up editor At first, I didn’t BOTher to get my pens in a bunch, but when the predictions got more dire, queries more persistent (journalists), book review promises accompanied by winks (friends), and mails in all-caps (editor), I had to do something. After a fair amount of whining and whinging, spiralling and venting, faffing and staying off the net (har har!), doodling and dreaming up delicious possibilities – my piece would go viral, the editor would offer me a weekly column in the vein of Mathrubhootham-meets-Mrs FunnyBones, my Instagram follower count would skyrocket to four digits – I got down to thinking about artificial intelligence and natural intelligence and creating books for kids. My two bitcoins? Kidlit creators (KC) will win the war against AI. There, I said it. Before you do the customary eye roll and go, “That’s what delulu dinosaurs thought before the asteroid hit”, hang on a New York minute. Everyone and their aunt are going on and on about AI posing a threat to us, but is it really? Because last I checked, AI wasn’t exactly creating stuff, merely curating it. Ergo, it still needs people to create original content, so it can dutifully rip it off. If anything, AI is kind of like the Uber of the literary world: It doesn’t actually own the vehicle (copyright). It heavily relies on independent drivers (creators) and uses their vehicles – without their consent – to give a ride to other literary travellers Travellers can hail the vehicle for a ride, but they can’t really pass it off as their own. Not without serious legal consequences. As Anthropic recently found out after losing a copyright case. Even as I type this, they are shelling out a modest 1.5 billion dollars as a settlement to a group of authors for using pirated versions of their books to train their chatbot, Je m’appelle Claude. And Bloomsbury, the publisher of the Harry Potter franchise, are laughing all the way to the bank with a million-pound payout. KC – 1, AI – 0. On to the next. Let me make a sweeping statement (because, why not) about the kidlit community. Making books for children of all ages is not just our profession. It’s our vocation. It’s that siren call which must be answered, that itch which must be scratched, that beast which must be fed, distractions – deadlines, diapers, doomscrolling, Donald dissing – notwithstanding. Believe you, me. We are not in it for the money (there isn’t any) or fame (unless you count getting accosted at grand literature festivals, only to be asked, “Excuse me, can you tell me where the toilets are?” as fame) or glitz and glamour (let’s face it, only Zendaya can pass off tatty sweatpants as high fashion) or because it’s “easy” (you please try entertaining a seven-year-old who’d rather play Roblox) or because we want to eventually write for grown-ups (some of us do that parallelly, thanks very much) or because we want to impart morals and values and raise a generation of sanskaari robots. We create books for children because we love it. We love pulling all-nighters, hunched over our laptops while the rest of the world Netflixes and chills. We love sacrificing family outings, nights out in town with friends and personal grooming-fitness-wellness to dream up wildly exciting stories, scenes and scenarios. We love working ourselves into a frenzy while we are at it – why, the sales of Eno shot through the roof during the writing of this piece alone. And we love doing it over and over, even though the whole world says “kids aren’t reading anymore and parents only ever spend on textbooks” and “children’s literature has a slightly higher crud percentage than literature as a whole” and “why does India have over one hundred literature festivals when it doesn’t have enough readers”. Agrees illustrator, graphic designer and author Sharanya Kunnath, “Increasingly I have been wanting the tactility of actual materials to appear in my work, perhaps as pushback against AI in some part, but also because they genuinely are more joyful to work with. It’s not an immediate process; there’s no undo button, you need to plan properly, you have to wait for things. I don’t see AI as competition in terms of quality; it is competition in terms of speed. There is absolutely no comparison with the vitality of something made by a human being, even if it’s a distracted doodle at the edge of a newspaper.” KC – 2, AI – 0 Big reveal: Hate. Intolerance. Fake news. Wars. Prejudice. Oppression. Climate change. Inflation. Information overload. Brain rot. Digital fatigue. Family reunions. WhatsApp uncles. Anti-national accusations. You name it – it’s how we deal with it. To paraphrase SRK in Devdas , who on earth creates kidlit to escape the world? We create kidlit to be able to bear it. Somehow, I doubt AI feels strongly about any of what’s happening around us. Oh, that’s right. Machines, software, code, algorithms can’t feel. KC – 3, AI – 0 Hope you’re keeping score, dear gentle reader. Anyhoo, enough of the dark stuff. Creating books for kids is what we do for fun. Use AI to brainstorm ideas, outline the story, craft scenes, churn out the entire plot, fact-check (good luck with that!), meet deadlines, or, like in one famous instance, to come up with the musical tastes of the protagonist? Where’s the fun in that? Adds lawyer-turned-award-winning author Mallika Ravikumar, “Recently I was asked to judge a writing competition. I was disappointed by what I saw. I had good reason to suspect that many of the entries had been written by AI. They were far too polished, robotic and grammatically perfect. But if someone wants to be original, authentic and heartfelt, AI is not going to help.” To counter the aforementioned challenge, Vinitha, author of Uma Kapoor vs The Universe, suggests, “We ought to wonder how we can go about boring children with AI. Because once you realise AI has no curiosity, no confusion, no joy in the struggle, it becomes terribly dull. The problem isn’t that kids are using AI. The problem is that we, as adults, have stopped being interesting enough to compete with it. We’ve stopped listening. We’ve stopped sitting with them in their confusion. We’ve handed them screens and then blamed them for liking them. If we want children to think for themselves, we have to show them that thinking is a sport, not a chore.” KC – 4, AI – 0 Also, remember the time when we could mug a TON (think: equivalent of terabytes) of useless information? Zillions of telephone numbers? And birthdays? And anniversaries? Without ever relying on a calendar/phone/notes/reminders/FB wall (strictly for Gen X)/another person’s self-congratulatory Instagram post? Now we can barely remember our door number. What if we let AI do all the heavy lifting for us, let tech do all the work, and the same thing happens to our creative impulses? What if we stop feeling the urge to put pen to paper, fingers to keyboard? Shudder. Mr Orwell couldn’t possibly have dreamt up a more disturbingly dystopic future. KC – 5, AI – 0 Besides, if AI creates something for us, is it even art? Correct me if I’m wrong (I’m not), but isn’t art something created by humans for other humans about what it means to be human? KC – 6, AI – 0 What’s that you say? What about creators who use AI but try to pass it off as authentic output, like those celebrities who drop dozens of apparel sizes overnight, and still deny ever popping Ozempic? Whatever happened to complete transparency and full disclosure? Worry not. Grim cautionary tales abound: International organisations conducting investigations to check if award-winning submissions are indeed human-produced. Big Five publishers withdrawing novels after allegations run rife that it’s AI slop. Creators losing book deals, readers, fans, face. So there. Perhaps kidlit publishers will incorporate a logo that tells human writing apart from AI slop on the cover, like the society of authors in the UK has, perhaps AI is the new reality and it’s not going away anywhere, perhaps artificial superintelligence will start mimicking us better, perhaps AI-generated books will flood the market, perhaps AI will clone itself and become independent of humans, but isn’t that how it’s always been? Every time there’s a new supervillain on the screen, er, scene – video games with their unlimited levels, World Wide Web with its countless pages, e-commerce with its dopamine hits, socials with their endless scrolling – there’s a great hoo-ha about the Postliterate Age. And yet, kidlit creators march on. Says author Richa Tilokani, whose book for middle-graders is forthcoming, “If this is the Age of AI, it’s all the more important that we think, create, engage, examine and articulate our feelings and encourage children to do the same. A world without original artists, writers, poets, thinkers and creators is poorer for it.” In the words of one of my favourite poets, Faiz Ahmed Faiz: “Hum parvarish-e-lauh-o-qalam karte rahenge/ Jo dil pe guzarti hai raqam karte rahege” “We shall continue putting pen to paper / We shall continue pouring out our hearts” We shall not trust AI systems to do most of our work as certain CEOs of tech behemoths would have us do. We shall treat AI like rejection: mope and move forward. And, of course, we shall place our faith in our young readers. We shall trust them to consume and create human-made books. Gen Z and Alpha may love their reels, memes, videos, short-form content and vasteguna-huiyas, but remember the last time someone underestimated them? Vibha Batra is an author, poet, adperson and hand-on-heart tech-neutral. Her 37th book, Saru and Sorry , was published recently.

article_title: India’s poorest will pay the most for ethanol-fuel push
sub_title: Gains of reducing vehicular emissions and fuel imports are undercut by the diversion of food resources, the toll on human bodies and cost of vehicle repairs.
article_content: I first learned to think about ethanol as a fault line in conversations with my friend Joan Martinez Alier, a political ecologist. We met in 1987, drawn together by a shared question: how much energy really goes into producing our food once you count what nature and human labour truly cost? My own interest was in the energetics of marine fisheries: the input-output balance of energy in that world. Ethanol was one of the clearest examples Alier used of that balance being falsified elsewhere. Energetics involved converting everything – a litre of diesel, an hour of a fisherman’s labour, a kilogramme of fish – into the same currency: the calories, or kilocalories, of energy each one represents. Simple bookkeeping can then be done: for every calorie that goes into fishing, how many calories of food come back out? When the return is high, the fishery is productive. When it costs more energy to catch the fish than what the fish give back as food, there is a deficit – even if the market still calls the catch a success. When I met, Alier he was writing about Brazil, whose ethanol programme, Proálcool, was being celebrated by economists as a triumph of energy planning. The programme, Alier pointed out, benefited the car-owning fifth of Brazilians. But its costs – water diverted from other uses, land turned over to cane and sugarcane workers whose life expectancy was shortened by brutal harvesting conditions – fell on people who never saw a drop of the fuel they were subsidising with their bodies and their land. He called this an ecological distribution conflict: where the gains from a resource are captured by one group while the losses are pushed onto another with no voice in the decision. That framework, which he explained in his book Ecological Economics: Energy, Environment and Society , has stayed with me. It is the lens through which India should look at its own ethanol programme. There are three hidden ledgers to India’s ethanol push: the diversion of food, the strain on water and land, and the uneven technical burden on the vehicle fleet. There is, of course, the debate over mileage loss, corroded fuel lines, E10 versus E20. But the central issue is who bears the weight of a policy being sold as a national benefit in a country that remains, by any honest reckoning, one of the hungriest, most polluted and most unequal societies on the planet. Cleaner mobility is driven by smarter resource management. Through diversified feedstocks, efficient irrigation, Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) distilleries and science-backed practices, India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme is advancing a more sustainable clean energy… pic.twitter.com/UVGKRS6ZWc In July, the government told Rajya Sabha that India’s three state-run oil marketing companies had purchased 705.43 crore litres of ethanol up till June 2026, for the ethanol supply year 2025-26, at a cost of Rs 49,577. In the last three years, the oil marketing companies had spent over Rs 1.72 lakh crore (roughly $20.6 billion) procuring ethanol . India also had 501 ethanol distilleries with a capacity approaching 16 billion litres annually. The government’s defense is that only surplus stocks are being diverted to make ethanol after food-welfare needs are met. This saves precious foreign exchange from being spent on crude oil imports while shielding farmers from price crashes. But look at the economics of that “surplus”. The Food Corporation of India procures rice from farmers at roughly Rs 44 per kg. That rice is then sold to ethanol distilleries at around Rs 23 per kg. So public money for food security is subsidising fuel for private vehicles. Meanwhile, the National Food Security Act underwrites free foodgrains for nearly 80 crore Indians and rice makes up roughly two-thirds of what they receive. Diverting rice toward ethanol, even at the margin, tightens a food system that covers a population larger than Europe. As maize is pulled into ethanol production as well, farmers are shifting away from pulses and oilseeds – the crops that provide essential nutrition to poor households. The result is a double burden: higher prices for essential food items and greater market volatility. A policy to manage surplus grain is, in practice, reshaping what the country grows and who can afford to eat well. It is also worth asking who controls this enterprise. India’s ethanol market is a mix of state-owned refineries and private conglomerates. But public-sector oil marketing companies are the sole purchasers of fuel-grade ethanol: they set prices, decide quotas and approve supplies. When the government sets a blending target, oil marketing companies are obliged to buy the ethanol to meet it, guaranteeing a market for private producers regardless of the social or environmental costs. Private producers capture the profits, public agencies absorb the market risk and the socio-ecological costs are dispersed onto the rest. Innovation is driving a more sustainable ethanol ecosystem. Modern ethanol plants are designed to promote resource efficiency through Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems, process water recycling and reuse. By combining advanced technologies with responsible resource management,… pic.twitter.com/KfXHVlkfIH The environmental costs of ethanol add to the food costs. Here, it helps to separate the two kinds of water sources. Green water is rainfall absorbed directly by soil. Blue water is surface and groundwater drawn for irrigation, which competes with drinking supplies and other demands in a water-stressed country. On this measure, India’s three main ethanol feedstocks look strikingly different: Rice: Monsoon rainfall means green water dominates nationally, but western and southern regions rely heavily on blue water pumped from aquifers. In India, it takes between 2,800 cubic metres per tonne and 3,500 cubic meters to produce a tonne of rice – more than double the global average of 1,325. Sugarcane: Sugarcane, which requires more than 1,500 cubic meters per tonne, relies heavily on blue water drawn continuously from rivers and aquifers in already water-stressed states like Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh. Maize: Maize in India is the most water-intensive relative to global benchmarks. India’s maize water footprint runs to roughly 2,500 cubic meters per tonne (against a global average of 1,220), largely because low hectare yields require vastly more water to produce a single tonne. 1.58 lakh crore paid to farmers under the Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme from Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2014–15 to 31 May 2026. Transforming farm produce into green fuel, India's ethanol blending programme is strengthening rural livelihoods while advancing the nation's clean… pic.twitter.com/bzmUpoTNvN Then there is land. Meeting India’s ethanol targets is expected to require diverting seven million hectares to eight million hectares of cropland. Land conversion on this scale risks pushing agriculture into the margins of forests, releasing stored soil carbon and undoing the climate benefits ethanol is meant to deliver. Combined with the intensive fertiliser and groundwater use for high-yield farming, India’s ethanol policy is reducing vehicular emissions while piling up ecological debt upstream. The human cost is severe. Across India’s sugarcane belt, harvesting is done manually, often in punishing heat. Studies document severe heatstroke and chronic kidney disease among agricultural labourers , a heavy health penalty that is omitted from cost-benefit analyses. Sugarcane cutting exacts such a severe physical toll that a true thermodynamic ledger must account for the energy cost of replacing the workforce – the premature deaths, chronic illness and bodies worn out before their time. The mechanical impact of ethanol similarly maps onto India’s socio-economic fractures. The impact of ethanol on an engine depends on whether its fuel system can automatically adjust to ethanol's lower energy density and corrosive properties. Vehicles built after April 2023 feature the Electronic Fuel Injection and upgraded materials, which means they adapt better to ethanol’s lower energy density and corrosive properties, suffering a modest 2% to 5% drop in efficiency. Older, carburetted vehicles cannot adjust. Their mileage drops by 15% to 20% while fuel lines swell and crack, and carburettors corrode, leaving owners to pay for out-of-pocket repairs without manufacturer retrofit support. India’s vehicle fleet is dominated by older automobiles used by the working-class and middle-class. Two-Wheelers are 70% to 75% of all registered vehicles in India, with an average working life of 12 to 15 years. The vast majority of two-wheelers on the road predate the 2023 Electronic Fuel Injection mandate and belong to delivery workers, commuters and traders for whom a two-wheeler is an economic necessity. Cars: Private cars are owned by 7.5% to 8% of Indian households. These owners skew wealthier and are far more likely to drive post-2023 fuel-injected vehicles. (While three-wheelers are rapidly shifting to electric drive, the two-wheeler majority remains bound to petrol.) Combine these three threads – food security, environmental strain, and vehicle mechanics – and it is evident that a policy aimed at financial and fuel efficiency is being paid for by Indians carrying the heaviest burdens: poor households dependent on public grain, water-stressed farming regions, and the two-wheeler-riding majority. Cleaner tailpipe combustion and reduced crude oil imports are genuine gains from the ethanol transition, but the social and ecological costs must also be considered. There are viable alternatives, like second-generation or 2G ethanol produced from agricultural waste, such as paddy straw and sugarcane bagasse, rather than food crops. India has demonstrated this potential with plants like Indian Oil’s 2G facility in Panipat. This technology is expensive and faces waste-logistics bottlenecks, but it does not compete with the dinner plate and nor does it demand that India’s most vulnerable citizens underwrite an energy transition they had no role in designing. John Kurien is a reflective development practitioner and former professor at the Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram.

article_title: Ashoka University and Oxford’s Balliol College announce a new £10,000 prize in creative nonfiction
sub_title: The prize will be given annually to the best book of creative nonfiction published anywhere in English, including translations.
article_content: The Centre for the Creative and the Critical, Ashoka University, and Balliol College, Oxford have announced The Ved Mehta International Prize in Creative Nonfiction , an international book award in creative nonfiction. The award has been established in honour of writer Ved Mehta and carries a cash prize of £10,000. It will be given annually to the best book of creative nonfiction published anywhere in English (including translations) in the preceding year. If a translated book is chosen, the translator also will receive a prize of £2,000. The first award will be given in 2026 for a book published in 2025. The shortlist will be announced in September, and the prize in November. The award ceremony will take place at Balliol and at Ashoka in alternate years. The award will be decided by a panel of three judges chosen by an international advisory board convened by Ashoka University and Balliol College. This year’s jury comprises professors Merve Emre and Seamus Perry, and Pulitzer-Prize winning author and academic Vijay Seshadri. The award is meant to recognise the more imaginative forms of nonfiction writing, and to acknowledge the stretching of genre-related boundaries in creative nonfiction. This may include memoir and autobiography, portraits of historians, philosophers, and theologians, criticism, travel writing, and political commentary. While these categories are not restrictive, they may all be considered. Ved Mehta (1934-2021) was a pioneer of many forms of creative nonfiction, ranging from memoir and autobiography to portraits of historians, philosophers, and theologians, as well as criticism and political commentary.

article_title: How a bureaucrat has forced Maharashtra’s eateries and other food businesses to clean up their act
sub_title: Tukaram Mundhe’s zero tolerance towards unsanitary kitchens and dark stores has won him fans – and unnerved the industry.
article_content: On August 8, a packed auditorium in Pune rose to applaud Tukaram Mundhe. Some took videos of the bureaucrat walking up to the stage. Others shouted out compliments. The event itself was titled “Unstoppable Tukaram”. Rarely has any bureaucrat appointed Maharashtra’s food and drug administration commissioner met with such public adulation. Since Mundhe took over in May, his crackdown on unhygienic practices in the food industry in the state has won him truckloads of admirers – and inspired social media memes. “He is going viral on social media,” said B Shami, who owns Crown Bakery in Mumbai. “And it has caused panic in our industry.” Under the bureaucrat’s instructions, food inspectors have scaled up surprise inspections. Not just that, they are handing out immediate suspension notices for serious violations, a departure from previous practices, officials told Scroll . “He is not afraid to go after big influential players,” said Omprakash Sadhwani, a retired joint commissioner of drugs in the food and drug administration. In the last three months, Domino’s and Pizza Hut outlets have been temporarily shut down after inspectors found cockroaches and expired products in their kitchens. Many of Mumbai’s legacy food businesses, from the K Rustom ice-cream parlour to Parsi Dairy and restaurants like Shalimar and Rehmania had their licences suspended for a few days for a range of violations – fungal growth on walls, presence of rats and cockroaches, food not covered by insect-proof meshes and failure to test drinking water for pathogens. All four businesses had their licences restored after they met hygiene standards. The FDA, under Mundhe, has not shied away from turning the scrutiny on dark stores of quick commerce giants like Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. Several were suspended after lizards, cockroaches and expired products were found on their racks. The series of crackdowns have made Mundhe a household name, so much so that actor Paresh Rawal took to social media platform X to urge Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis to ensure that the bureaucrat is not shunted out of his department. The 2005-batch IAS officer has a reputation for being an honest bureaucrat, unafraid to ruffle feathers. He has been transferred 25 times in over two decades. In some posts, he has spent only a few months. The Maharashtra FDA’s drive appears to have prodded similar action in neighbouring Karnataka, where inspection of five-star hotel kitchens and high-end restaurants also revealed shocking sanitary standards. While Mundhe has found a huge fan following, the food industry is unnerved. Several business owners have approached courts asking for relief. Many say that by handing out immediate suspension notices, he is skipping standard procedures. On August 18, the Bombay High Court said the food and drug administration was going “overboard” and directed it to pay Rs 5 lakh fine to a Pune sweet shop for not reinstating its licence despite a 98% adherence to hygiene. But former joint commissioner for food in Maharashtra, CB Pawar, told Scroll that the slew of strict measures were “not harsh”. Pawar added, defending Mundhe’s style of functioning, “The provisions under the Act allow FDA to suspend outlets. If a restaurant is unhygienic and not shut down, who will be responsible if people get food poisoning?” In the Pune outlet particularly, a complaint of food poisoning had been filed with the FDA and its food samples were found unsafe. At a press conference on Thursday, Mundhe said, “If there are observations made by the HC, we take it seriously. At the same time we make sure to follow the law. We are not exceeding our jurisdiction, we are following due process.” From people buying breakfast on the street to those ordering groceries on quick commerce apps, consumers are cheering Mundhe. In Sion, Vilas Singh, aged 24, first read about Mundhe on Instagram when the bureaucrat began suspending a few famous restaurants. Over the last few weeks, he has begun to see changes in local food stalls. “I usually have breakfast outside,” Singh said. “Earlier I would get vada pav or idli in a newspaper. Sometimes the newspaper ink would stain the food if it was too hot. Now they wrap it in butter paper.” Mundhe began his career in 2005 as an assistant collector in Solapur, and was later posted as the collector of the district in 2014. He is remembered for initiating multiple water conservation projects in Solapur to remove the dependence of several villages on water tankers. In 2016, Mundhe was given charge of the Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation, where he cracked down on illegal construction and unauthorised hawkers. While his work was appreciated by local residents, several politicians campaigned for his transfer and a no-confidence motion was passed by corporators against him. He was eventually moved out in less than a year without being assigned another posting. In 2020, the Uddhav Thackeray-led government posted Mundhe as Nagpur commissioner, where he cancelled several major tenders awarded by the previous commissioner. His method of working irked union minister Nitin Gadkari who complained to the Prime Minister’s Office against him. In an interview to The Hindu , Mundhe maintained that he followed three principles before he took any action – legality, public interest and whether his decision is morally correct. “If any two conditions are met – including legality – I act. There is no hesitation, no gradual approach, no negotiation with what is wrong simply because it is powerful,” he said. The food industry in Maharashtra has been taken aback by the new-found aggression in the food and drug administration’s methods. A food inspector told Scroll that before Mundhe took over, inspections were less frequent due to staff shortage. “We are working overtime now,” he said. The official said that Mundhe has instructed them to adhere to “zero-tolerance” for unsanitary conditions. On June 29, a food inspector conducted a surprise inspection in Pawan Bar and Restaurant in Navi Mumbai. According to the Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association, earlier food inspectors would “usually notify a restaurant before an inspection”. Now, most inspections are conducted without intimation. The inspection in Pawan Bar and Restaurant found hygiene-related lapses. The restaurant had a 63% compliance with requirements under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The next day the FDA issued a suspension notice to the restaurant. Two weeks later, in a re-inspection the restaurant had 100% compliance with all requirements. Even then, the FDA did not revoke its suspension. The restaurant finally approached the Bombay High Court, which revoked the suspension. The hotel’s kitchen remained shut for over 25 days. The lawyer representing the restaurant owner, Sagar Shetty, told Scroll that their main grievance was that the officials did not issue an improvement notice. Instead, they chose to immediately suspend the license. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, a food inspector can inspect a food outlet and issue an ‘improvement notice’. The notice points out violations and gives a period of two weeks to comply. In cases where a food operator fails to comply, the inspector can suspend their license after a showcause notice. The Act also gives the FDA power to immediately suspend a licence “in the interest of public health”. It is this provision that Mundhe’s team has opted for in several cases. Across Maharashtra, the licences of at least 10 hotels have been suspended in the last three months immediately after inspection, said Vijay Shetty, president of Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association, or AHAR. Ashwini Ranjane, assistant commissioner for food, said it was well within the rights of the food inspector to suspend licences. “A food inspector can immediately make out if a place is unsanitary by just looking at a restaurant’s kitchen,” she said. Ranjane added that the FDA gives improvement notices in 70% to 80% cases of minor violations – if record keeping is poor, if employees’ medical records are not maintained, or if minor hygiene lapses are seen. “Immediate suspension is issued when during our visits, we see dirt everywhere,” she said. “If there are major issues and multiple violations that the operator needs to work on and that is not possible to achieve in a few days, we have to suspend them.” In July, food inspectors found expired flavouring agents and essence, rats and houseflies in K Rustom’s ice-cream parlour. In the century-old Parsi Dairy, fungus was found on the walls and raw materials found lying on the floor. Despite the presence of rats and flies, the food was left uncovered. The licences of both outlets were suspended temporarily. Parsi Dairy was able to reopen after about 10 days after a re-inspection was undertaken. K Rustom decided to renovate its over 70-year-old store. An FDA officer said their licence has also been reinstated. “If the food can directly harm the health of customers, then we can suspend the licence immediately,” a retired joint commissioner of food from Maharashtra told Scroll . Several bakery owners protested against a blanket suspension of licence following “minor violations” during inspections. In July, the FDA issued stop-business notices to four bakeries after finding “hygiene related lapses”, expired raw materials and unsanitary cooking conditions. In videos that FDA shared, the New Maharashtra bakery in Chembur had fungus on baking trays and its walls.
